title: Grassfire: does a fire front across a meadow read as its own regime?
question: Watching the fire run along the sward -- does that read as a distinct fast surface fire, different in kind from a tree burning, or just as fire moving through some plants?
context_md:
WP-B3 acceptance item 4, the last one. Grass is meant to be the fastest fuel in the world: the thing that carries a fire across open ground between two stands.

**Measured first, in a paired test over identical strips** -- time for a front to cross 170 cells:

| surface | frames | speed |
|---|---|---|
| **grass** | **127** | **1.34 cells/frame** |
| tree foliage | 161 | 1.06 |
| leaf litter | 180 | 0.94 |
| bare soil | never crossed | — |

So grass is ~27% faster than canopy foliage, and bare soil stops a front dead. That part is settled by number, not by eye.

**What I want your eye on is whether it *reads* as a different regime in motion**, which no number can answer.

**One finding worth knowing before you watch it, because it surprised me.** The first attempt showed *nothing* — the ignition landed (the counter said 10 cells lit) and the fire went straight out. The cause was not moisture, which was my first guess; it was **connectivity**. Fire spreads to 4-neighbours only, and at 64 founders the sward has gaps between tufts that a front cannot cross. At 200 founders it is continuous and the fire runs the whole world.

That means a **patchy meadow is a firebreak and a closed one is a fuse**, emergently, from no rule that says so. If that seems right to you it is worth keeping; if grass should carry fire even when sparse, that is a real design call and I have not made it.
